title: Types of Classes in Java - GeeksforGeeks
content:
A class in Java is a blueprint that defines the data and behavior of objects. It can contain fields, methods, constructors, nested types, and initialization blocks.

  • Objects are created as instances of classes.
  • Classes support important OOP concepts such as encapsulation, inheritance, and abstraction.

Declaring a Class in Java

A basic class declaration contains the class keyword followed by the class name and class body.

class ClassName {
    // Fields
    // Constructors
    // Methods
}

A class can contain:

  • Fields
  • Methods
  • Constructors
  • Initialization blocks
  • Nested classes
  • Nested interfaces
  • Enums and records as nested types
Java 
class Student {
    int id;
    String name;

    public static void main(String[] args)
    {
        Student student = new Student();

        System.out.println(student.id);
        System.out.println(student.name);
    }
}

Output
0
null

Explanation: Here, Student is a class and student is an object of that class. Because the fields are not explicitly initialized, Java assigns their default values.

Types of Classes in Java

Classes are commonly described based on their purpose and modifiers. Some important types are:

Note: These categories are not mutually exclusive. For example, a POJO can also be a final class, and a concrete class can also be a nested class.

1. Final Class

A class declared using the final keyword is called a final class.

The main purpose of final on a class is to prevent inheritance.

final class Vehicle {
}

Another class cannot extend it:

class Car extends Vehicle {
}

The above code causes a compilation error because Vehicle is final.

Important Point: Declaring a class final does not make its objects immutable.

For example:

final class Student {
    String name;

    void setName(String name) {
        this.name = name;
    }
}

Although Student cannot be extended, its name field can still be changed.

Therefore:

  • final class cannot be subclassed.
  • final method cannot be overridden.
  • final variable cannot be reassigned after initialization.

Immutability is a separate design concept. A truly immutable class must prevent its observable state from changing after object creation.

Java 
final class Base {
    void display()
    {
        System.out.println("Method of Base class");
    }
}

class GFG {
    public static void main(String[] args)
    {
        Base obj = new Base();
        obj.display();
    }
}

Output

Method of Base class

2. Static Nested Class

Java does not allow a top-level class to be declared static.

However, a class declared inside another class can be declared static. Such a class is called a static nested class.

class Outer {
    static class Nested {
    }
}

Unlike a non-static inner class, a static nested class does not require an instance of the outer class.

Important Points

  • Only nested classes can be declared static.
  • A static nested class can contain both static and instance members.
  • Objects of a static nested class can be created.
  • It cannot directly access non-static members of the outer class without an outer-class object.
Java 
class Outer {

    static int value = 100;

    static class Nested {

        int number = 10;

        void display()
        {
            System.out.println("Value: " + value);
            System.out.println("Number: " + number);
        }
    }
}

class GFG {
    public static void main(String[] args)
    {

        Outer.Nested obj = new Outer.Nested();
        obj.display();
    }
}

Output

Value: 100
Number: 10

3. Abstract Class

A class declared using the abstract keyword is called an abstract class.

An abstract class:

  • Cannot be instantiated directly.
  • Can contain abstract methods.
  • Can contain concrete methods.
  • Can have constructors.
  • Can contain static methods and fields.
  • Can contain final methods.
  • Can implement interfaces.

An abstract class does not need to contain an abstract method.

Java 
interface X {
    int product(int x, int y);
}

abstract class Product implements X {

    public int product(int x, int y) { return x * y; }
}

class GFG extends Product {

    public static void main(String[] args)
    {

        GFG obj = new GFG();

        int result = obj.product(20, 10);

        System.out.println("Product: " + result);
    }
}

Output

Product: 200

4. Concrete Class

A concrete class is a class that can be instantiated and does not leave any required abstract methods unimplemented.

A concrete class can:

  • Have fields and methods.
  • Extend another concrete class.
  • Extend an abstract class after implementing the required abstract methods.
  • Implement one or more interfaces.
Java 
class Calculator {

    int sum(int x, int y) { return x + y; }
}

class GFG {
    public static void main(String[] args)
    {

        Calculator obj = new Calculator();

        System.out.println("Sum: " + obj.sum(10, 8));
    }
}

Output

Sum: 18

5. POJO Class

POJO stands for Plain Old Java Object. It is a simple Java class used to represent application data without depending on any specific framework.

A POJO may contain:

  • Fields
  • Constructors
  • Getter and setter methods
  • Other application-specific methods

Getters, setters, private fields, or a no-argument constructor are not mandatory for a class to be considered a POJO.

Java 
class Student {

    private int id;
    private String name;

    Student(int id, String name)
    {
        this.id = id;
        this.name = name;
    }

    public int getId() { return id; }

    public String getName() { return name; }
}

class GFG {
    public static void main(String[] args)
    {

        Student student = new Student(101, "Rahul");

        System.out.println(student.getId());
        System.out.println(student.getName());
    }
}

Output

101
Rahul

6. Singleton Class

A Singleton class is designed so that an application normally uses only one instance of that class while providing a controlled way to access it.

A typical Singleton implementation contains:

  • A private constructor.
  • A private static reference to the instance.
  • A public static method for obtaining the instance.
Java 
class Singleton {

    private static Singleton instance;

    private Singleton() {}

    public static Singleton getInstance()
    {

        if (instance == null) {
            instance = new Singleton();
        }

        return instance;
    }
}

class GFG {
    public static void main(String[] args)
    {

        Singleton obj1 = Singleton.getInstance();
        Singleton obj2 = Singleton.getInstance();

        System.out.println(obj1 == obj2);
    }
}

Output

true

7. Nested and Inner Classes

Java allows one class to be declared inside another class. Such classes are generally called nested classes.

Nested classes are broadly divided into:

  1. Static nested classes
  2. Inner classes

An inner class is specifically a non-static nested class.

Inner classes can be further classified as:

  • Member inner class
  • Local inner class
  • Anonymous inner class

Therefore, a static nested class should not technically be described as an inner class.

A. Member Inner Class

A non-static class declared directly inside another class is called a member inner class.

It can access the members of its enclosing object, including private members.

Java 
class Outer {

    private int value = 100;

    class Inner {

        void show()
        {
            System.out.println("Value: " + value);
        }
    }
}

class GFG {
    public static void main(String[] args)
    {

        Outer outer = new Outer();
        Outer.Inner inner = outer.new Inner();

        inner.show();
    }
}

Output

Value: 100

B. Anonymous Inner Class

An anonymous inner class is an unnamed class declared and instantiated in a single expression.

It is commonly used when a small one-time implementation of a class or interface is required.

Example 1: Using a Class

Java 
class Parent {

    void show() { System.out.println("Parent method"); }
}

class GFG {

    public static void main(String[] args)
    {

        Parent obj = new Parent() {
            @Override void show()
            {
                System.out.println(
                    "Anonymous class method");
            }
        };

        obj.show();
    }
}

Output

Anonymous class method

Example 2: Using an Interface

Java 
interface Hello {
    void show();
}

class GFG {

    public static void main(String[] args)
    {

        Hello obj = new Hello() {
            public void show()
            {
                System.out.println("Anonymous class");
            }
        };

        obj.show();
    }
}

Output

Anonymous class

C. Static Nested Class

A class declared static inside another class is a static nested class.

Java 
class Outer {

    static int data = 100;

    static class Nested {

        void show() { System.out.println("Data: " + data); }
    }
}

class GFG {
    public static void main(String[] args)
    {

        Outer.Nested obj = new Outer.Nested();
        obj.show();
    }
}

Output

Data: 100

D. Local Inner Class

A class declared inside a block, commonly inside a method, is called a local class or local inner class when it is non-static.

Java 
class Outer {

    void outerMethod() {

        System.out.println("Outer Method");

        class Inner {

            void innerMethod() {
                System.out.println("Inner Method");
            }
        }

        Inner obj = new Inner();
        obj.innerMethod();
    }
}

class GFG {

    public static void main(String[] args) {

        Outer obj = new Outer();
        obj.outerMethod();
    }
}

Output

Outer Method
Inner Method
